source_text: Danielem prophetam juxta Septuaginta interpretes, Domini Salvatoris ecclesiæ non legunt, utentes Theodotionis editione : et hoc cur acciderit, nescio. Sive enim quia sermo Chaldaicus est, et quibusdam proprietatibus a nostro eloquio discrepat, noluerunt Septuaginta interpretes easdem lineas in translatione servare, sive sub nomine eorum ab alio nescio quo non satis Chaldæam linguam sciente, editus est liber : sive aliud quid causæ extiterit ignorans : hoc unum affirmare possum, quod multum a veritate discordet, et recto judicio repudiatus sit. Sciendum quippe Danielem maxime, et Esdram Hebraicis quidem litteris, sed Chaldæo sermone conscriptos, et unam Jeremiæ pericopen : Job quoque cum arabica lingua habere plurimam societatem. Denique et ego adulescentulus post Quintiliani et Tullii lectionem ac flores rethoricos, cum me in linguæ hujus pistrinum reclusissem : et multo sudore, multoque tempore vix cœpissem anhelantia, stridentiaque verba resonare, et quasi per cryptam ambulans, rarum desuper lumen aspicerem, impegi novissime in Danielem : et tanto tædio affectus sum, ut desperatione subita omnem laborem veterem voluerim contemnere. Verum, adhortante me quodam Hebræo, et illud mihi crebrius in sua lingua ingerente:, "Labor improbus omnia vincit" : et qui mihi videbar sciolus, inter Hebræos cœpi rursum discipulus esse Chaldaicus. Et ut verum fatear, usque ad præsentem diem magis possum sermonem Chaldaicum legere, et intellegere, quam sonare. Hæc idcirco refero, ut difficultatem vobis Danielis ostenderem : qui apud Hebræos nec Susannæ habet historiam, nec hymnum trium puerorum, nec Belis draconisque fabulas : quas nos, quia in tote orbe dispersæ sunt, veru anteposito, easque jugulante subjecimus : ne videremur apud imperitos magnam partem voluminis detruncasse. Audivi ego quendam de præceptoribus Judæorum, cum Susannæ derideret historiam, et a Græco nescio quo eam diceret esse confictam, illud opponere quod Origeni quoque Africanus opposuit, etymologias has ἀπὸ τοῦ σχοίνου σχοίσαι, καί ἀπὸ τοῦ πρίνου πρίσαι, de Græco sermone descendere. Cujus rei nos intelligentiam nostris hanc possumus dare : ut verbi gratia, dicamus de arbore illice dixisse eum, "ilico pereas" : et a lentisco, "in lentem te comminuat angelus" : vel "non lente pereas" : aut "lentus, id est flexibilis ducaris ad mortem" : sive aliud ad arboris nomen conveniens. Deinde tantum fuisse otii tribus pueris cavillabatur, ut in camino æstuantis incendii metro luderent : et per ordinem ad laudem Dei elementa omnia provocarent, aut quod miraculum divinæque adspirationis indicium, vel draconem interfectum offa picis, vel sacerdotum Belis machinas deprehensas : quæ magis prudentia sollertis viri, quam prophetali essent spiritu perpetrata ? Cum vero ad Habacuc veniret, et de Judæa in Chaldeam raptum discophorum lectitaret, quærebat exemplum ubi legissemus in toto veteri testamento quemquam sanctorum gravi volasse corpore, et in puncto horæ tanta terrarum spatia transisse, cui cum quidam e nostris satis promptulus ad loquendum promptulus, Ezechielem adduxisset in medium, et diceret eum de Chaldæa in Judeam fuisse translatum, derisit hominem, et ex ipso volumine demonstravit Ezechielem in spiritu se vidisse transpositum. Denique et Apostolum nostrum, videlicet ut eruditum virum, et qui legem ab Hebræis didicisset, non fuisse ausum affirmare se raptum in corpore, sed dixisse: "Sive in corpore sive extra corpus : Nescio, Deus scit" [2. Cor. 12.]. His et talibus argumentis apocryphas in libro Ecclesiæ fabulas arguebat. Super qua re lectoris arbitrio judicium derelinquens, illud admoneo, non haberi Danielem apud Hebræos inter prophetas, sed inter eos qui Hagiographa conscripserunt. In tres siquidem partes omnis ab eis scriptura dividitur : in legem, in prophetas, et in hagiographa, id est in quinque, et octo, et undecim libros : de quo non est hujus temporis disserere. Quæ autem ex hoc propheta, immo contra hunc librum Porphyrius objiciat : testes sunt Methodius, Eusebius, et Apollinaris, qui multis versuum millibus ejus vesaniæ respondentes, nescio an curioso lectori satisfecerint. Unde obsecro vos O Paula et Eustochium, fundatis pro me ad Dominum preces : ut quamdiu in hoc corpusculo sum, scribam aliquid gratum vobis, utile Ecclesiæ, dignum posteris. Præsentium quippe judiciis oblatrantium non satis moveor : qui in utramque partem, aut amore labuntur, aut odio.
thought_title: Why the Church reads Daniel in Theodotion's version, and Jerome's own struggle with Aramaic
orientation: Jerome is addressing Paula and Eustochium in his preface to Daniel, explaining why the Church does not read Daniel according to the Septuagint and defending his own translation from the Hebrew.
pass_a_gloss: The churches of the Lord Savior do not read the prophet Daniel according to the Septuagint interpreters, using Theodotion's version: and why this has happened, I do not know. For either because the language is Aramaic, and it differs from our speech by certain peculiarities, the Septuagint interpreters did not want to preserve the same lines in translation, or under their name a book was published by someone else I know not who, not sufficiently knowing the Aramaic language: or some other cause existed, I being ignorant: this one thing I can affirm, that it disagrees much from the truth, and has been rejected by right judgment. Indeed one must know that Daniel especially, and Ezra, were written with Hebrew letters indeed, but in Aramaic speech, and one passage of Jeremiah: Job also has very much kinship with the Arabic language. Finally I too as a young man, after the reading of Quintilian and Tully and the flowers of rhetoric, when I had shut myself into the mill of this language: and with much sweat, and much time, had scarcely begun to make the panting, and hissing words resound, and as if walking through a crypt, to glimpse a rare light from above, I stumbled at last upon Daniel: and I was affected with such weariness, that in sudden desperation I wished to despise all my old labor. But, a certain Hebrew urging me, and thrusting upon me more frequently in his own language: 'Unceasing labor conquers all things': and I who seemed to myself a bit of a know-it-all, among the Hebrews began again to be a student of Aramaic. And to confess the truth, up to the present day I can read Aramaic speech, and understand it, more than pronounce it. I report these things for this reason, to show you the difficulty of Daniel: who among the Hebrews has neither the story of Susanna, nor the hymn of the three youths, nor the fables of Bel and the dragon: which we, because they are scattered throughout the whole world, have subjoined with a spit placed before, and it slaying them: lest we seem to have cut off a great part of the volume among the unskilled. I heard a certain one of the teachers of the Jews, when he ridiculed the story of Susanna, and said it was invented by some Greek I know not who, oppose that which Africanus also opposed to Origen, that these etymologies, 'from the reed to tear you' and 'from the holm-oak to saw you', descend from Greek speech. Of which matter we can give this understanding to our people: so that for example, we may say concerning the tree 'ilice' he said, 'ilico may you perish': and from the mastic tree, 'may the angel crush you slowly': or 'may you not perish slowly': or 'O slow one, that is pliable, may you be led to death': or something else fitting the name of the tree. Then he jested that the three youths had so much leisure, that in the furnace of blazing fire they played in meter: and in order they called all the elements to the praise of God, or what miracle and sign of divine inspiration was it, either the dragon killed by a lump of pitch, or the devices of the priests of Bel detected: which were accomplished more by the prudence of a clever man, than by prophetic spirit? But when he came to Habakkuk, and read of the tray-bearer snatched from Judea into Chaldea, he sought an example where we had read in the whole old testament that any of the saints had flown with a heavy body, and in a point of an hour crossed such great spaces of lands. When a certain one of ours, quite ready to speak, had brought Ezekiel into the midst, and said that he had been transferred from Chaldea into Judea, he mocked the man, and from the very volume demonstrated that Ezekiel saw himself transported in spirit. Finally also our Apostle, namely as a learned man, and one who had learned the law from the Hebrews, had not dared to affirm that he was snatched in body, but said: 'Whether in the body or out of the body: I do not know, God knows' [2 Cor. 12]. With these and such arguments he accused the apocryphal fables in the church's book. Leaving the judgment on this matter to the reader's decision, I warn this, that Daniel is not held among the Hebrews among the prophets, but among those who wrote the Writings. For indeed all scripture is divided by them into three parts: into the Law, into the Prophets, and into the Writings, that is into five, and eight, and eleven books: about which it is not of this time to discuss. But what Porphyry objects against this prophet, or rather against this book, Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris are witnesses, who responding to his madness with many thousands of verses, I do not know whether they have satisfied the curious reader. Wherefore I beseech you, O Paula and Eustochium, pour out prayers for me to the Lord: that as long as I am in this little body, I may write something pleasing to you, useful to the Church, worthy for posterity. For I am not sufficiently moved by the judgments of those barking at the present: who slip into either side, either by love or by hatred.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'the Septuagint' for Septuaginta interpretes; 'juxta' means 'according to' in this context of reading a version
Glossary requires 'Theodotion's version' for Theodotionis editio
Glossary requires 'Aramaic' for Chaldæus sermo; here sermo Chaldaicus is the same term in different word order

choices.english: have subjoined with a spit placed before, and it slaying them
choices.why: Literal rendering of the obelus metaphor: the spit (veru) is placed before the additions and slays them, marking them as not in the Hebrew
rejected: prefixed a mark and subjoined them as if killing them

choices.why: Literal genitive: the book belonging to the church, i.e. Daniel as read in church; avoids the ambiguous 'book of the Church'
rejected: in the book of the Church

pass_b_english: The churches of the Lord Savior do not read the prophet Daniel according to the Septuagint; they use Theodotion's version. Why this happened, I do not know. Whether it was because the language is Aramaic and differs from our speech in certain peculiarities, and the Septuagint translators did not wish to preserve the same lines in translation; or whether the book was published under their name by someone else, I know not who, who did not know Aramaic well enough; or whether some other cause existed, I am ignorant. This one thing I can affirm: it differs greatly from the truth and was rightly rejected. One should know that Daniel especially, and Ezra, were written in Hebrew letters but in the Aramaic language, as was one passage of Jeremiah; Job also has much affinity with the Arabic tongue. Finally, when I was a young man, after reading Quintilian and Tully and the flowers of rhetoric, I shut myself up in the mill of this language. With much sweat and much time I had scarcely begun to make the panting, hissing words resound, and as if walking through a crypt I glimpsed a rare light from above, when at last I stumbled upon Daniel. I was seized with such weariness that in sudden despair I wanted to throw away all my old labor. But a certain Hebrew urged me on, and kept repeating to me in his own language, "Hard work conquers all." And so I, who had seemed to myself a mere smatterer, began again to be a student of Aramaic among the Hebrews. To confess the truth, even to this day I can read and understand Aramaic better than I can pronounce it. I mention these things to show you the difficulty of Daniel, who among the Hebrews has neither the story of Susanna, nor the hymn of the three youths, nor the fables of Bel and the dragon. These we have subjoined with a spit placed before them, which, as it were, runs them through, because they are scattered throughout the whole world, lest we seem to have cut off a large part of the volume among the unlearned. I heard a certain one of the teachers of the Jews, when he ridiculed the story of Susanna and said it was invented by some Greek or other, raise the objection that Africanus also raised against Origen: that these etymologies, "from the mastic tree, to split you" and "from the oak to saw you," derive from the Greek language. We can give our own people an understanding of this matter, so that, for example, we may say that from the holm-oak he said, "May you perish at once," and from the mastic tree, "May the angel crush you to a lentil," or "May you not perish slowly," or "O slow one, that is, pliable one, may you be led to death," or something else suited to the name of the tree. Then he mocked the three youths for having so much leisure that they played in meter in the furnace of the blazing fire and called upon all the elements in order to praise God; or what miracle or sign of divine inspiration, he asked, was it that a dragon was killed with a lump of pitch, or that the devices of the priests of Bel were detected? Were these things accomplished more by the shrewdness of a clever man than by a prophetic spirit? And when he came to Habakkuk and read repeatedly of a dish-bearer carried off from Judea to Chaldea, he asked for an example where we had read in the whole Old Testament that any of the saints had flown with a heavy body and crossed such great stretches of land in a moment of time. When one of our own, quite ready to speak, brought Ezekiel forward and said that he had been transferred from Chaldea to Judea, he ridiculed the man and showed from that very volume that Ezekiel had seen himself transported in the spirit. Finally, he argued that our Apostle too—a learned man, to be sure, who had learned the law from the Hebrews—had not dared to affirm that he was carried off in the body, but had said, "Whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know; God knows" (2 Corinthians 12:2). With these and similar arguments he was attacking the apocryphal fables in the church's book of Daniel. Leaving judgment on this matter to the reader's discretion, I give this warning: Daniel is not counted among the Prophets by the Hebrews, but among those who wrote the Writings. For all Scripture is divided by them into three parts: the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings—that is, into five, eight, and eleven books. But this is not the time to discuss that. As for what Porphyry objects against this prophet, or rather against this book, Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris are witnesses, who answered his madness with many thousands of lines—whether they satisfied the curious reader, I do not know. Therefore I beg you, Paula and Eustochium, to pour out prayers for me to the Lord, that as long as I am in this little body I may write something pleasing to you, useful to the Church, worthy of posterity. For I am not much moved by the judgments of those who bark at me in the present, who slip into one side or the other either from love or from hatred.

problems.why: Latin has ablative absolute 'veru...jugulante' (spit slaying), not 'it slaying them'; 'easque' is object of subjecimus.
problems.fix: with a spit placed before them, slaying them as we subjoined them

problems.why: 'jugulante' is ablative singular agreeing with 'veru' (the spit), not a separate clause.
problems.fix: and, with it slaying them, subjoined them
problems.ruling: 'jugulante' is ablative absolute/participle with 'veru', not 'it slaying' as separate clause; grammar misread.

problems.quote: May you perish on the spot
problems.why: 'ilico' means 'immediately, on the spot,' but Jerome's point is the wordplay on 'ilice' (holm-oak): 'may you perish from the holm-oak.'
problems.fix: may you perish from the holm-oak
problems.ruling: 'ilico pereas' is Jerome's Latin wordplay on 'ilice' (holm-oak); 'on the spot' loses the pun entirely.

problems.quote: May the angel crush you slowly
problems.why: 'lentem' here means 'lentil' (from lens), not 'slowly'; the wordplay is on lentiscus (mastic tree) and lens (lentil).
problems.fix: may the angel crush you to a lentil
problems.ruling: 'lentem' = lentil (from lens); Jerome's wordplay on lentiscus/lens is lost by rendering 'slowly' instead of 'lentil.'

problems.why: 'lente' here continues the lentil wordplay, not 'slowly'; should be 'may you not perish to a lentil' or similar.
problems.fix: may you not perish to a lentil
problems.ruling: 'lente' continues lentil wordplay from lentiscus/lens, not 'slowly'; meaning is changed.

fixed: Corrected 'and it slaying them' to 'slaying them as we subjoined them' to reflect the ablative absolute 'veru...jugulante' modifying the action of subjoining.
Corrected 'May you perish on the spot' to 'May you perish from the holm-oak' to preserve the wordplay on 'ilice' (holm-oak) and 'ilico'.
Corrected 'May the angel crush you slowly' to 'May the angel crush you to a lentil' to preserve the wordplay on 'lentem' (lentil) from 'lentiscus' (mastic tree).
Corrected 'May you not perish slowly' to 'May you not perish to a lentil' to preserve the lentil wordplay in 'lente'.

problems.quote: May you not perish to a lentil
problems.why: Latin 'non lente pereas' means 'may you not perish slowly', not 'to a lentil'.

problems.quote: May you not perish to a lentil
problems.why: lente = 'slowly' here, not 'lentil'. The pun is: 'may you not perish slowly.'
problems.ruling: Source 'non lente pereas' puns on 'lentus' (slow/pliable), not 'lens' (lentil). 'Lentil' breaks wordplay.

problems.quote: slaying them as we subjoined them
problems.why: Latin has ablative absolute 'veru anteposito' (spit having been placed before), not 'slaying them as we subjoined them'.
problems.fix: with a spit placed before them, killing them as we subjoined them
problems.ruling: 'veru anteposito, easque jugulante' = 'with a spit placed before, slaying them'; English 'slaying them as we subjoined them' mistranslates both ablatives absolute.

problems.why: Latin 'discophorum' means 'one carrying a dish/basket', but 'lectitaret' is from 'lectito' (to read often/repeatedly), not 'carried off'. The Hebrew teacher reads about Habakkuk repeatedly.
problems.ruling: 'discophorum lectitaret' = 'read repeatedly about the tray-bearer'; English 'a tray-bearer carried off' drops 'lectitaret' (read repeatedly) entirely.

problems.quote: Finally, our Apostle too—a learned man, to be sure, who had learned the law from the Hebrews—did not dare to affirm that he was carried off in the body, but said, "Whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know; God knows" (2 Corinthians 12:2).
problems.source_quote: Denique et Apostolum nostrum, videlicet ut eruditum virum, et qui legem ab Hebræis didicisset, non fuisse ausum affirmare se raptum in corpore, sed dixisse
problems.why: The accusative and infinitive continues the Jewish teacher’s argument; English states it as Jerome’s own claim.
problems.fix: Finally he added that our Apostle too—a learned man, taught the Law by the Hebrews—had not dared to say he was caught up in the body, but had said, "Whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know; God knows" (2 Corinthians 12).
problems.ruling: "non fuisse ausum affirmare... dixisse" is accusative-infinitive, still the Jewish teacher's reported argument ("Denique" continues "His et talibus argumentis"); English makes it Jerome's own assertion.

fixed.note: The English repeats 'subjoined' and breaks the sentence; jugulante modifies the spit (obelus) that 'slays' the additions.

fixed.fix: from the mastic tree, to split you
fixed.note: The pun is on σχῖνος (mastic tree, matched by Jerome's lentiscus) and σχίσαι (split), so 'reed' is wrong, and so is the checker's 'oak'.

dismissed.why: Paul says 'raptum' (caught up/taken up), not 'carried off'; and the Jewish teacher cites Paul as not daring to affirm he was 'raptum in corpore'.
dismissed.note: 'Carried off' is a fair rendering of raptum and matches the earlier 'carried off' used of Habakkuk.

last_rejected.why: per ordinem means one after another; English in order to is purpose and drops the sequence.
last_rejected.fix: and summoned all the elements, one after another, to the praise of God
last_rejected.ruling: "per ordinem ... provocarent": "called upon all the elements in order to praise God" is a natural rendering; "in order" and purpose ad laudem are both conveyed, minor ambiguity only.

last_rejected.quote: with a spit placed before them, which, as it were, runs them through
last_rejected.why: Jerome prefixed an obelus (spit) and subjoined them as if killing/stabbing them; 'subjoined... with spit placed before' garbles; 'jugulante' means the spit kills them. Reasonably close, but 'runs them through' is fine; the 'because' clause attaches wrongly.
last_rejected.fix: We have subjoined them, with a spit placed before them as if to run them through, because they are scattered throughout the whole world, lest we seem to have cut off...
last_rejected.ruling: “veru anteposito, easque jugulante subjecimus” is kept; “quia… dispersae sunt” still explains why they were subjoined, with “ne” as purpose.
